01

Setting specification

Task

Minimize $f$ globally over $\mathbb{R}^d$ and return a point with small objective gap.

Admissible model

$f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}$ is differentiable and satisfies $\|\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y)\|_2\le\beta\|x-y\|_2$ for every $x,y\in\mathbb{R}^d$.

$f$ is convex throughout the ambient space.

A global minimizer $x_*\in B_2(0,R)$ exists; the localization ball does not restrict the function domain.

Oracle interface

At any finite query point $x$ in $\mathbb{R}^d$, the oracle returns the single exact scalar $f(x)$. The reply is uniquely determined and contains no gradient, subgradient or derivative-vector product.

The public inputs are $d$, $\beta$, $R$, $\varepsilon$, together with the sets, kernels and auxiliary operations explicitly declared above. Information about the unknown objective and any undisclosed sample distribution is obtained only through the stated interface.

Output

Return $\widehat{x}\in \mathbb{R}^d$. The output may be an unqueried point, an average or convex combination that remains in the stated space. No function value, gradient, inner solution, or accuracy certificate must accompany the output.

Loss or accuracy criterion

The base loss is $\ell(I,x)=f(x)-f_*$, where $f_*=\inf_{u\in \mathbb{R}^d}f(u)$. This nonnegative loss is evaluated at the output, with tolerance $\varepsilon$.

Resource accounting

Each scalar function value or noisy observation costs $1$ call. Every location in a multipoint finite difference, every initialization query, and every reference observation is charged.

Only the declared oracle resource is charged. Computation and storage using existing information, together with explicitly known geometric and proximal operations, are free.

Algorithm views and success guarantees

Deterministic

Only deterministic strategies are allowed. Queries, stopping and postprocessing may be arbitrary measurable adaptive functions of the history. No linear-span or zero-respecting restriction is imposed.

Interactions are sequential, and every actual response in a batch is charged separately. Except for explicitly listed auxiliary interfaces, arithmetic, linear algebra, storage, and internal computation on available information are free, with no additional communication or memory restriction. Finite-difference steps must be finite and positive; real-number precision is not charged separately.

After fixing the public inputs, choose one algorithm that works for every admissible instance and reply law. The requirement $\ell(I,\widehat{x})\le \varepsilon$ holds deterministically for each instance.

Oracle cost uses a deterministic worst-case budget: $N\le T$ on every possible execution path. For multiple resources, coordinatewise caps apply jointly along the same path.

Randomized

Private randomization is allowed, with the seed independent of the instance and external randomness. Queries, stopping and postprocessing may be arbitrary measurable adaptive functions of the history. No linear-span or zero-respecting restriction is imposed.

Interactions are sequential, and every actual response in a batch is charged separately. Except for explicitly listed auxiliary interfaces, arithmetic, linear algebra, storage, and internal computation on available information are free, with no additional communication or memory restriction. Finite-difference steps must be finite and positive; real-number precision is not charged separately.

After fixing the public inputs, choose one algorithm that works for every admissible instance and reply law. The error requirement is $\Pr(\ell(I,\widehat{x})\le \varepsilon)\ge2/3$.

Probability is over the algorithm's random seed only.

Oracle cost uses a deterministic worst-case budget: $N\le T$ on every possible execution path. For multiple resources, coordinatewise caps apply jointly along the same path.

Output qualification. Random selection among previously queried points is permitted, subject to the declared success guarantee.

Used only at derivative orders and on regions where the model guarantees its existence.

$\|\cdot\|_{\mathrm{op}}$

Euclidean induced matrix or tensor operator norm

Domain
Take the supremum over Euclidean unit input vectors of the corresponding order.

$\|T\|_{\mathrm{op}}=\sup_{\|u_1\|_2,\ldots,\|u_j\|_2\le1}|T[u_1,\ldots,u_j]|$

$\mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{fun}},\mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{out}},\mathcal{X}$

Function domain, admissible output domain and optimization domain

Domain
Each is the Euclidean space or subset explicitly specified in this profile

$\mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{out}}=\mathbb{R}^d$ and $\mathcal{X}=\mathbb{R}^d$; the function domain is the region on which the model imposes regularity.

$N^*$

Optimal worst-case oracle complexity satisfying the complete guarantee

Domain
$N^*\in[0,+\infty]$

Take the infimum over admissible algorithms, followed by the worst case over the instances of this profile. With multiple resources, use this scalar only for an explicitly specified resource projection.

$x_*$

A global minimizer or quadratic center whose existence is promised by the model

Domain
Belongs to the localization domain specified here; used only under the stated existence promise

The full-space minimizer is unique in the strongly convex class. The center of a positive semidefinite quadratic model need not be unique.

/proofs/0/body · SHA-256 a5c82ebecf3e082953aacf639f4db3a9a8f3308adc30992dbe0443ce0608e13e
Writing $\gamma=1-2/Q\in(0,1/2)$, $$T_{\mathrm{det}}=\Theta(d),\qquad T_{\mathrm{rand},2/3}=\Theta(\max\{1,d\gamma\}).$$ The constants are uniform in $d,Q$, and in every declared strong-convexity lower budget $0<\mu\le\beta$. Let $g=\nabla f(0)$. The convex function $h(x)=f(x)-\langle g,x\rangle$ is minimized at zero. A $1/\beta$ descent step for $h$ from a minimizer $x_*$ of $f$ gives $$f(0)-f_*\le R\|g\|-\|g\|^2/(2\beta).$$ For a rank-$k$ orthogonal projector $P$, central differences in an orthonormal basis of its range yield $\widehat g=Pg+e$ with $e\in\operatorname{range}(P)$ and $\|e\|\le\beta h\sqrt{k}/2$. At $\widehat x=-\widehat g/\beta$, cancellation of the cross term in the smoothness inequality gives $$f(\widehat x)-f_*\le R\|g\|-\frac{\|g\|^2+\|Pg\|^2}{2\beta}+\frac{\|e\|^2}{2\beta}\le\frac{\beta R^2}{2(1+a)}+\frac{\|e\|^2}{2\beta},\quad a=\frac{\|Pg\|^2}{\|g\|^2}.$$ The zero-gradient case satisfies the same error estimate. For a Haar-uniform subspace choose $k=\min\{d,\max\{24,\lceil4d\gamma\rceil\}\}$. If $k<d$, then $\mathbb E a=k/d$ and $\operatorname{Var}(a)=2k(d-k)/(d^2(d+2))\le2k/d^2$. Thus $\Pr(a<k/(2d))\le8/k\le1/3$, and $k/(2d)\ge2\gamma$. For $k=d$, $a=1\ge2\gamma$ deterministically. Set $$m(\gamma)=(1-\gamma)-(1+2\gamma)^{-1}>0,\qquad h=R\sqrt{m(\gamma)/k}.$$ This finite positive step makes the displayed error strictly less than $\varepsilon$ on the good event. It uses $2k$ values. Taking $P=I$ gives the deterministic $O(d)$ upper bound. For the randomized lower bound take $f_v(x)=\beta\|x-v\|^2/2$, with $v$ uniform on $R S^{d-1}$. A value reveals at most one linear projection of $v$. After at most $T<d$ adaptive projections, the unrevealed part remains conditionally uniform on the residual sphere; the revealed squared energy $S$ obeys $\mathbb E S\le TR^2/d$. If $S<\gamma R^2$, a success ball of radius $R\sqrt{1-\gamma}$ covers at most half that residual sphere. Consequently $p_{\rm success}\le1/2+T/(2d\gamma)$, forcing $T\ge d\gamma/3$. Zero calls are impossible because the success balls for $v=\pm Re_1$ are disjoint and cannot both receive probability $2/3$. For a deterministic algorithm with $T<d$, answer $\beta(\|x\|^2+R^2)/2$. Choose a length-$R$ vector $v$ orthogonal to every queried vector. The objectives $f_v$ and $f_{-v}$ give the same adaptive transcript, but their average loss at the common output is at least $\beta R^2/2>\varepsilon$. Their Hessian is $\beta I$, so the lower family also belongs to every strongly convex budget $\mu\le\beta$ and to the unknown-quadratic class.

The endpoint lower bound at $Q=3$ yields $\Omega(d)$ for every $Q\ge3$. The deterministic finite-difference accelerated bound is $O(d)$ on every fixed numerical interval $4\le Q\le128^2$. Solving to a smaller error also solves to any larger error, so minimax complexity is nondecreasing as $\varepsilon$ decreases. At $Q=3$, the endpoint lemma gives $\gamma=1/3$ and hence a uniform $\Omega(d)$ randomized lower bound. The deterministic accelerated upper bound $O(d\sqrt Q)$ is at most $128$ times its universal constant on the stated interval. The same upper bound applies to randomized algorithms. The endpoint hard family is already quadratic, so the lower statement transfers unchanged to the quadratic subclass; the quadratic upper follows by restriction of the smooth algorithm.

For the smooth class, $Q\ge128^2$ gives $\Omega(d\log Q)$. This also holds in a public strongly convex class with $\kappa\ge2$. For a ball-restricted Lipschitz class, $A=LR/\varepsilon\ge6\cdot128^2$ gives $\Omega(d\log A)$. Dorn et al., Theorem 2.5, gives $$\frac{3d}{4000}\left[1+\frac{\log(\beta_hR_h^2/\varepsilon)}{\log((\beta_h+\mu_h)/(\beta_h-\mu_h))}\right]$$ when $\mu_h/\beta_h\in[1/2,1]$ and $\beta_hR_h^2/\varepsilon\ge128^2$. Choose $\mu_h=\beta_h/2$, so the denominator is $\log3$. A convex $\beta$-smooth class contains this subclass with $\beta_h=\beta$, $R_h=R$. A public lower curvature budget $\mu\le\beta/2$ also contains it, uniformly in the public condition number. For the ball-restricted Lipschitz class choose $R_h=R/2$, $\beta_h=2L/(3R)$, and $\mu_h=\beta_h/2$. On $B_2(R)$, $\|\nabla f(x)\|\le\beta_h(\|x\|+\|x_*\|)\le L$, and the global minimizer remains inside the feasible ball. One source value simulates one restricted value. The stronger source oracle permits all such algorithms, and $Q_h=A/6$. The explicit window makes $\log(A/6)$ and $\log A$ uniformly comparable. For a selected-component finite sum with all components equal to the same hard function, one component query is one source query. This transfer has cost one, not $n$. A logarithmic and a dimension-dependent lower bound may be maximized only where both respective windows hold.

/proofs/3/body · SHA-256 e337fe1bbdc7a8471c27bff8578ac9695fda39f5bd738324501658aee12cbc83
A public feasible point whose objective gap is at most $G_0$ solves every target $\varepsilon\ge G_0$ with exactly zero calls. For a convex mean objective that is $L$-Lipschitz on a ball of radius $R$, the center has gap at most $LR$. A sample Lipschitz modulus $G$ with $\mathbb E G^r\le L^r$, $r>1$, implies $\mathbb E G\le L$, so the same certificate applies to moment models. Integrability at one point ensures that the mean is defined. If a globally $\beta$-smooth objective has a global minimizer within distance $R$ of the public initial point, its gradient vanishes at that minimizer and the smoothness inequality gives gap at most $\beta R^2/2$. In a declared norm, use the corresponding radius in that norm. For $B_p(R)$ with Euclidean regularity this radius is $R$ when $p\le2$ and $R d^{1/2-1/p}$ when $p\ge2$. For a known positive semidefinite quadratic matrix $A$, the center has gap at most $\lambda_{\max}(A)R^2/2$; if $A=0$, the loss is identically zero. A public initial-gap promise $\Delta$ directly gives the certificate $G_0=\Delta$. For the Markov potential $r_0$, its companion initial iterate has gap at most $\mu r_0$. These are different certificates with different model assumptions; in particular, an unknown matrix with no public spectral bound does not acquire a uniform certificate. Call counts are nonnegative. Together with the stated algorithm, this proves exact zero complexity on each certified region. The upper/lower ratio is undefined, so it is stored as null rather than as $0/0$.

d is an integer >=1; beta>0, R>0, epsilon>0; Q=beta R^2/epsilon>0.
